reason: The sources thoroughly detail Gamma Cassiopeiae's rapid rotation, disk ejection, evaporation of IC 59/63, and the 2026 XRISM breakthrough across multiple independent sites.
story: Gamma Cassiopeiae forms the central peak of Cassiopeia's iconic celestial W, but beneath its familiar glow lies a volatile stellar engine. Rotating at an astonishing 450 kilometers per second—right on the brink of structural breakup—this massive powerhouse has flattened into an oblate spheroid and flung off huge sheets of gas into a surrounding equatorial decretion disk. Its blistering ultraviolet radiation is actively vaporizing nearby interstellar clouds, including the Ghost of Cassiopeia nebula. For five decades, astronomers were haunted by another riddle: the star blazed with high-energy X-rays fueled by 150-million-degree plasma. In 2026, the XRISM space observatory finally unmasked the culprit. The X-rays are not emitted by Gamma Cassiopeiae itself, but by a hidden white dwarf companion the size of Earth that silently siphons gas from the runaway disk.
angle: Gamma Cassiopeiae spins so fast it flings off its own gas disk, which is secretly devoured by an Earth-sized white dwarf companion to unleash 150-million-degree X-rays while vaporizing neighboring ghost nebulae.

claims.claim: Gamma Cassiopeiae marks the central point of the W-shaped asterism in the constellation Cassiopeia.
In 1866, Italian astronomer Angelo Secchi discovered hydrogen emission lines in Gamma Cassiopeiae, making it the first recognized Be star.
Gamma Cassiopeiae is located approximately 550 light-years away from Earth.
The star spins at an estimated true rotational velocity of roughly 450 km/s, close to its breakup speed.
Rapid rotation has distorted Gamma Cassiopeiae into an oblate shape with a pronounced equatorial bulge.
The star's extreme spin and high luminosity eject matter into a circumstellar equatorial decretion disk.
Gamma Cassiopeiae is an eruptive variable star that serves as the prototype for the Gamma Cassiopeiae variable star class.
During shell episodes, changes in the circumstellar disk cause irregular brightness fluctuations across historical extremes between magnitude 1.6 and 3.4.
Gamma Cassiopeiae radiates approximately 19,000 times more energy than the Sun.
Ultraviolet radiation from Gamma Cassiopeiae is actively evaporating and eroding the nearby nebulae IC 59 and IC 63.
Astronomers discovered in the mid-1970s that Gamma Cassiopeiae produces unusually hard, luminous X-rays.
The system produces X-ray emissions up to 40 times stronger than expected for typical massive B-type stars.
The X-ray emission arises from extremely hot plasma reaching temperatures exceeding 60 to 150 million degrees.
In 2026, the XRISM space telescope solved the 50-year X-ray mystery by tracking Doppler shifts in the hot plasma's orbital motion.
XRISM proved the X-rays are produced by a hidden white dwarf companion accreting material from the primary star's gas disk.
The white dwarf companion has a mass comparable to the Sun packed into a sphere roughly the size of Earth.
The primary star and its white dwarf companion form a spectroscopic binary system with an orbital period of about 203.5 days.
The star received the Apollo navigation nickname Navi, created by spelling astronaut Virgil Ivan Grissom's middle name backwards.

disputed: Evolutionary phase: S1 describes the star as a subgiant exhausting core hydrogen, whereas S5 notes that despite subgiant spectral signatures, it is modeled as an active hydrogen-fusing main sequence star. A script should state that while classified spectrally as a subgiant, models suggest it remains in its main-sequence core-burning phase.

Binary orbit eccentricity: S1 notes an eccentricity near zero (circular orbit), while S7 lists an eccentricity of 0.26. A script should adopt the newer circular orbit consensus or simply state the orbital period without specifying eccentricity.
Primary star mass: S1 gives 17 solar masses, while S5 gives around 15 solar masses. A script should describe the primary star generally as 15 to 17 times the mass of the Sun.

Naming origin of Navi: S1 states the name was bestowed by the Apollo 9 crew and Dr. Clarence Cleminshaw (not Grissom himself), whereas S4 attributes the playful reversal directly to Grissom. A script should state the nickname honors astronaut Gus Grissom by reversing his middle name Ivan, avoiding specific attribution of who first coined it.
